content: Research indicates that the number of individuals with intellectual disabilities who are becoming parents is increasing. While intellectual disabilities do not inherently lead to parenting difficulties, they may affect a person's ability to parent effectively. Children of parents with intellectual disabilities may face a higher risk of neglectful care, which can result in health issues, developmental delays, behavioral problems, or an increased likelihood of intellectual disability. Additionally, parents with intellectual disabilities are more likely to be involved in child protection or care proceedings compared to other parents. The objective of this research was to evaluate the effectiveness of parent training interventions specifically designed for parents with intellectual disabilities. These interventions aim to support parenting skills, improve parent-child relationships, ensure safe parenting practices, and foster a positive family environment. A comprehensive search was conducted in July 2017 across multiple databases, including CENTRAL, Ovid MEDLINE, Embase, and CINAHL, as well as two trial registries. Reference lists of relevant studies were reviewed, and experts in the field were contacted to identify additional ongoing or unpublished studies. The inclusion criteria for the review were randomized controlled trials (RCTs) and quasi-RCTs that compared parent training interventions for parents with intellectual disabilities to either standard treatment or a control group. Standardized Cochrane methods were used for data collection and analysis. As of July 2017, four trials involving 192 participants met the inclusion criteria. Most participants were mothers, with only seven fathers included across two studies. The children involved ranged in age from one month to six years and five months. The studies were conducted in Australia, Canada, the Netherlands, and the USA, each evaluating a different intervention with varying outcomes. Three of the interventions were delivered in the participants' homes, while one was conducted in a community setting, such as a church. The duration of the interventions ranged from seven weeks to 12 months and included training in practical childcare skills, home safety, and improving parents' responsiveness to their children. Parents in the control groups generally received standard treatment, and most were offered the intervention after the study concluded. Funding for the studies came from various sources, including the Ontario Mental Health Foundation, the Alabama Development Disabilities Council, the Best Practice Parenting Education Initiative, and ZonMw, The Netherlands Organisation for Health Research and Development. Due to the heterogeneity of the studies, a meta-analysis could not be performed. The quality of evidence, as assessed using the GRADE system, ranged from very low to moderate. Primary Outcomes: None of the studies reported on the attainment of specific parenting skill targets. One study, involving 30 parents, provided very low-quality evidence of improvements in parents' knowledge of life-threatening emergencies, their ability to recognize dangers, and their ability to implement safety precautions. This study also found limited evidence that parent training improved parents' understanding of child health, safe use of medications, recognition of child illness and symptoms, and seeking medical advice. Another study, involving 22 mothers, reported very low-quality evidence of improved skills related to childcare and safety in the intervention group. Secondary Outcomes: One study, involving 40 mothers, reported very low-quality evidence of improved maternal-child interaction at a 12-month follow-up after parent training. Another study, involving 83 mothers and 2 fathers, provided moderate-quality evidence that participation in the intervention group led to a greater reduction in parenting stress related to the child compared to the control group. One study, involving 22 participants, reported very low-quality evidence regarding child retention. Before the program, 82% of families with a previous child had experienced child removal by child protection authorities due to maternal maltreatment. After participating in the program, this figure dropped to 19%, with only one mother in this group having had a previous child removed. No studies reported data on outcomes such as the return to independent care of the child or the lifting of child-related court orders. Conclusions: There is some very low-quality evidence suggesting that parents with intellectual disabilities, particularly mothers, can provide adequate parenting when they receive appropriate training and support to develop necessary parenting skills. However, there is a lack of research exploring how these interventions work, for whom they are most effective, and under what circumstances. Notably, there is limited research involving fathers with intellectual disabilities or studies that consider the perspectives of the parents themselves. Larger RCTs with longer follow-up periods are needed to draw more definitive conclusions about the effectiveness of parent training interventions for this population.
